\begin{document}
\title{Supplementary Material for\\
``Payoff Allocation in Energy Community Games under Non-convex
Operations: A Duality-based Perspective''}
\author{Seokwoo Kim,~\IEEEmembership{Member,~IEEE,}
Yuin Moon,~\IEEEmembership{Member,~IEEE,}
Mohammad Reza Hesamzadeh,~\IEEEmembership{Senior Member,~IEEE,}
Jan Kronqvist,~\IEEEmembership{Member,~IEEE,}
Dong Gu Choi,~\IEEEmembership{Member,~IEEE}}
% \markboth{IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON ENERGY MARKETS, POLICY, AND REGULATION,~Vol.~xx, No.~xx, xx~2026}%
% {Kim \MakeLowercase{\textit{et al.}}: Supplementary Material}
\maketitle
This supplementary material has two parts.
Section~\ref{sec:sup_data} collects the data of the numerical study, that
is, the parameters of the community dispatch model, the asset
composition of the four communities, and the asset matrix of each
member. Section~\ref{sec:sup_stoch} writes out the two-stage stochastic
extension. Section, equation and proposition numbers without an ``S''
prefix refer to the main paper.

%% =====================================================================
% \section{Example}
% \label{sec:sup_ex}
% What Corollary~\ref{cor:cos} leaves open is whether $\omega^{*}$ is zero at all.
% The following two instances differ in a single parameter and answer it both ways.

% \begin{example}[Three prosumers and one threshold]
% \label{ex:threshold}
% Three prosumers each own $e$\,MWh of generation and one electrolyzer, which
% consumes exactly $2$\,MWh when committed and produces hydrogen worth $\$3$, and
% consumes and produces nothing otherwise. Electricity is bought outside at
% $\$2$/MWh and sold outside at $\$0$/MWh. There is a single period, no reserve
% product and no peak charge, so the only linking row is the internal electricity
% balance. With $y_j\in\{0,1\}$ indicating commitment, $q_j$ the electricity
% prosumer $j$ buys inside the community, $i_j\ge0$ its outside purchase and
% $s_j\ge0$ its spillage, the dispatch problem of a coalition $S$ is
% \begin{subequations}\label{eq:ex}
% \begin{align}
% &(\mathrm{DP}_S):\ \max_{y,q,i,s}\ \textstyle\sum_{j\in S}\big(3y_j-2i_j\big),
% \label{eq:ex_obj}\\
% &\mathrm{s.t.}\ \ e+q_j+i_j=2y_j+s_j,\quad \forall j\in S, \label{eq:ex_bal}\\
% &\hspace{2.1em} \textstyle\sum_{j\in S}q_j=0, \label{eq:ex_link}\\
% &\hspace{2.1em} y_j\in\{0,1\},\ i_j\ge0,\ s_j\ge0,\quad \forall j\in S,
% \label{eq:ex_bin}
% \end{align}
% \end{subequations}
% and Assumption~\ref{as:pool} holds, the linking row \eqref{eq:ex_link} being
% additive with a zero right-hand side.

% Take $e=2$ first, so that each prosumer meets the threshold on its own. A
% coalition of size $s$ commits all $s$ units from its own generation, buys nothing
% and spills nothing, so $v(s)=3s$ and every coalition is worth $\$3$ per member.
% The equal split $\chi_j=3$ satisfies $\ssum_{j\in S}\chi_j=v(s)$ for every $S$
% and is therefore efficient and stable. Relaxing $y_j$ to $[0,1]$ changes nothing,
% since the generation covers any $\ssum_jy_j\le3$, so
% $\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DWR}_N)=9=\vdp{N}$ and the vanishing gap certifies the
% nonempty core without any proper coalition being evaluated.

% Now set $e=1$, so that two prosumers are needed to fill one unit. A single
% prosumer holds $1$\,MWh and must buy $i=1$ to commit, earning $3-2=\$1$, while
% not committing earns $\$0$. A pair holds $2$\,MWh and commits one unit with
% $i=0$, earning $\$3$, whereas committing both units would require $i=2$ and earn
% $6-4=\$2$. The grand coalition holds $3$\,MWh and commits two units with $i=1$,
% earning $6-2=\$4$, against $\$3$ for one unit and $9-6=\$3$ for three. Hence
% \begin{equation}
% v(1)=1,\qquad v(2)=3,\qquad v(3)=4,
% \label{eq:ex_values}
% \end{equation}
% worth $\$1$, $\$1.5$ and $\$1.33$ per member. No efficient allocation is stable.
% If $\ssum_{j\in N}\chi_j=4$, adding the three pair requirements
% $\chi_1+\chi_2\ge3$, $\chi_1+\chi_3\ge3$ and $\chi_2+\chi_3\ge3$ counts every
% prosumer twice and gives $\ssum_{j\in N}\chi_j\ge4.5$, a contradiction.
% Equivalently, the balanced family placing weight $\tfrac12$ on each pair covers
% every prosumer exactly once and collects $\tfrac12(3+3+3)=4.5>4$, so the core is
% empty. The minimum of $(\mathrm{OPAP})$ is attained at $\chi=(1.5,1.5,1.5)$,
% giving $\alpha^{*}=4.5$, $\omega^{*}=0.5$ and $\varepsilon^{*}=\tfrac16$.

% That balanced family is the mixture of Remark~\ref{rmk:gap_core} made concrete. A
% prosumer commits in one of its two pairs and stays idle in the other, so the
% translation there places $\lambda_j$ half on a committed and half on an idle
% schedule. Relaxing $y_j$ to $[0,1]$ in \eqref{eq:ex_bin} buys exactly that
% schedule and yields $\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DWR}_N)=4.5$, attained at
% $\ssum_jy_j=1.5$, so here $\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}=\omega^{*}$ and
% \eqref{eq:cos_bound} holds with equality.
% \end{example}

% The two instances differ only in $e$, and the difference acts through waste. With
% $e=2$ every coalition fills a whole number of units. With $e=1$ a pair fills one
% unit exactly, whereas the grand coalition holds $3$\,MWh against a requirement of
% either $2$ or $4$ and must pay $\$2$ to close a shortfall worth $\$1.5$. That
% loss of $\$0.5$ falls on the grand coalition and not on the pairs, which is what
% places $\$1.5$ above $\$1.33$ and empties the core. Assumption~\ref{as:pool}
% holds throughout, with linking rows that are additive and homogeneous, so it
% delivers the bound of \eqref{eq:cos_bound} but no guarantee of a nonempty core.
% And since the waste is a matter of how the pooled generation divides by the
% threshold rather than of how many members share it, $\omega^{*}$ need not
% decrease in $n$ even though $\varepsilon^{*}=\omega^{*}/n$ does. The equality
% reached in Example~\ref{ex:threshold} is likewise a feature of its size, and
% Section~\ref{sec:num} reports communities in which $\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}$
% exceeds $\omega^{*}$.
%% =====================================================================
\section{Data of the Numerical Study}
\label{sec:sup_data}
This section reports the data of the numerical study in three parts: the
parameters of the dispatch model, which are common to all four
communities; the asset composition of each community; and the asset
matrix of each individual member.
\subsection{Parameters of the Community Dispatch Model}
\label{sec:sup_params}
Table~\ref{tab:params} reports every parameter of the dispatch model of
Section~III-B of the main paper. All entries are held fixed across the four
community sizes, so that the size axis varies $n$ alone. 
The electrolyzer is a three-state unit. Besides on and off it holds a
standby state that draws $1\%$ of its rating, which is cheaper than a
cold restart but not free, and a return from off costs $50$~\euro. Its
minimum load is $15\%$ of capacity, which lies within the range of $10$
to $16\%$ reported for PEM units. The standby draw is below the $2.5$ to
$5\%$ reported in the same literature, so the unit is modelled as
cheaper to park than a typical installation. If anything this
understates the value of commitment and with it $\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}$.
The power-to-hydrogen curve is concave and is represented exactly by six
segments with segment-selection binaries.
The heat pump is a two-state unit. It is committed between $20\%$ and
$80\%$ of its rating at a constant coefficient of performance of $3.28$,
and each start costs $10$~\euro. Its reserve headroom is available only
while it is on, which is why its contribution is measured in electric MW
while its operating window is on heat output.
Electricity storage is sized relative to its owner rather than in
absolute terms: rated power is a quarter of the asset capacity of the
owner and energy capacity is three times that power, so it scales with
the assets that member operates. Hydrogen and heat storage are sized
once for the community, so every member owning one holds the same
rating. Demand is that of $700$ households. The
community is a price taker and faces an import price $1.5$ times its
export price.

\subsection{Composition of the Four Communities}
\label{sec:sup_comp}
Table~\ref{tab:composition} counts the members that own each asset type
at each community size. The $n=60$ community doubles every count at
$n=30$ exactly, so these two sizes differ in $n$ and in nothing else.
The smaller communities do not match them in every share, because the
asset mix at $n=6$ and $n=15$ was set by role rather than by proportion.
The $n=6$ community holds no hydrogen or heat storage, so those two rows
begin at $n=15$.
What is held across all four sizes is the last row, which counts the
members that carry commitment binaries and stays near one third. These
are the members that generate $\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}$, so the flatness of
$\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}$ in $n$ is not confounded by a non-convex share
that drifts with $n$.

\subsection{Member Configurations}
\label{sec:sup_config}
Table~\ref{tab:config} reports the asset matrix of every member. The
four communities are nested, so the first $6$, $15$ and $30$ rows are the
$n=6$, $n=15$ and $n=30$ communities unchanged. At $n=6$ every function
is held by a single archetype. Member u1 owns wind with electric
storage, u2 an electrolyzer, u3 a heat pump, and u4 to u6 are
non-flexible consumers, one per carrier. Every coalition value at that
size can therefore be traced to a named role. The members added at
$n=15$ and $n=30$ introduce competition within each role, members that
own generation and conversion together, standalone storage operators,
and consumers active in two carriers.
The last column of Table~\ref{tab:config} gives the capacity multiplier
applied to each member added at $n=60$. Every added member differs from
the archetype it mirrors, so the community is not a two-fold replica of
the 30-prosumer one. A replica would shrink the core toward the
competitive allocation by the Debreu--Scarf theorem, and the comparison
across sizes in the main paper would measure that effect instead of the
effect of community size.

\section{Two-Stage Stochastic Extension}
\label{sec:sup_stoch}
Remark~\ref{rmk:stoch} of the main paper states that relaxing
Assumption~\ref{as:env}(iv) leaves the construction of
Section~\ref{sec:duality} intact. This section writes out the dispatch
problem and the Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation to which that remark refers,
constructs from them an allocation that settles scenario by scenario, and
verifies the claim.
\subsection{Decision Stages}
\label{sec:sup_stages}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set of scenarios of the renewable production,
the load, and the external market prices, with probabilities
$\rho_{\omega}>0$ and $\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}=1$. Every
parameter the scenario carries is indexed accordingly: the production
and load bounds of \eqref{eq:bnd_pd} are read as
$\underline p_{jt}^{k,\omega},\overline p_{jt}^{k,\omega}$ and
$\underline d_{jt}^{k,load,\omega},\overline d_{jt}^{k,load,\omega}$,
the first of these carrying the renewable availability and the second
the load. The electrolyzer states
$z_{jt}^{G,on},z_{jt}^{G,sb},z_{jt}^{G,off}$ with their transition
indicators, and the community reserve capacities $r_i^{sym}$, are decided
before the realization. Every remaining decision is taken after it: the
electrolyzer is redispatched within its committed state, so that the
segment selectors $\hat z_{jlt}^{\omega}$ and the segment inputs
$\hat d_{jlt}^{\omega}$ carry a scenario index, and so do the heat pump
input, the storage schedule, the reserve contributions, the community
exchanges, and the peak $p^{\omega}$.

Prices are revealed with the rest of the scenario. Import and export
prices therefore carry a scenario index, $\pi_t^{k,imkt,\omega}$ and
$\pi_t^{k,emkt,\omega}$, and so does the willingness to pay
$\bar u_{jt}^{k,\omega}$, which in Section~\ref{sec:setup} is the avoided
cost of buying the carrier outside and so moves with the import price.
Production costs $\bar c_{jt}^{k}$ and the peak tariff $\delta^{peak}$
are technology and network parameters and stay deterministic.
Assumption~\ref{as:env}(iii) is read scenario by scenario,
$\pi_t^{k,imkt,\omega}\ge\pi_t^{k,emkt,\omega}$ for every $\omega$,
which is what \eqref{eq:bnd_size} needs in order to keep
$\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}}$ bounded while leaving every coalition
value unchanged. We further take the scenario prices to lie in a compact
set fixed in advance, so that refining the scenario set adds outcomes
without widening the range of prices any single outcome may take;
Proposition~\ref{prop:sup_stoch}(c) is stated under this reading.
 
The reserve capacity price is a special case. Since $r_i^{sym}$ is sold
before the realization and cannot be revised, a scenario-dependent
$\pi_i^{res,\omega}$ enters the objective only through its mean
$\bar\pi_i^{res}:=\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}\pi_i^{res,\omega}$,
and its dispersion is immaterial to the model. We write $\bar\pi_i^{res}$
from here on.
 
Market trades are treated as recourse, which is the price-taking
counterpart of Assumption~\ref{as:env}(ii): the community adjusts its
external position after the realization at the prices it faces. Its
exposure to price uncertainty is therefore carried by the two first-stage
decisions alone, the unit being committed and the reserve capacity sold
before any price is known. Within a scenario the second stage sees the
whole day at once, so the trading value it reports is an upper bound on
what a multistage model would return. A day-ahead position settled
against a separate balancing price is the sharper alternative. It adds a
first-stage trade block to each prosumer and an imbalance term to the
objective, and leaves every structural statement below unchanged, so we
keep the simpler form.
\subsection{Dispatch Problem}
For a coalition $S\subseteq N$,
\begin{subequations}\label{eq:sup_dp}
\begin{align}
&(\mathrm{DP}_S^{\Omega}):\ \max\
\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}\Big[\ssum_{j\in S}\ssum_{k\in K}\ssum_{t\in T}
\big(\pi_t^{k,emkt,\omega}e_{jt}^{k,mkt,\omega} \nonumber\\
&\quad-\pi_t^{k,imkt,\omega}i_{jt}^{k,mkt,\omega}
+\bar u_{jt}^{k,\omega}d_{jt}^{k,load,\omega}-\bar c_{jt}^{k}p_{jt}^{k,\omega}\big)
-\delta^{peak}p^{\omega}\Big] \nonumber\\
&\quad-\ssum_{j\in S}\ssum_{t\in T}c_j^{G,su}z_{jt}^{G,su}
+\ssum_{i\in I}\bar\pi_i^{res}r_i^{sym}
\label{eq:sup_dp_obj}
\end{align}
subject to the community-level linking constraints, imposed in every
scenario,
\begin{align}
&\ssum_{j\in S}\big(i_{jt}^{k,com,\omega}-e_{jt}^{k,com,\omega}\big)=0,
&&\forall t,k,\omega \label{eq:sup_bal}\\
&r_i^{sym}\le\ssum_{j\in S}r_{jt}^{u,\omega},\quad
 r_i^{sym}\le\ssum_{j\in S}r_{jt}^{d,\omega},
&&\forall i,\,t\in T_i,\,\omega \label{eq:sup_res}\\
&\ssum_{j\in S}\big(i_{jt}^{E,mkt,\omega}-e_{jt}^{E,mkt,\omega}\big)\le p^{\omega},
&&\forall t,\omega  \label{eq:sup_peak}
\end{align}
and, for every $j\in S$, to the prosumer-level constraints
\eqref{eq:pb_E}--\eqref{eq:bin} of the main paper, written for each
$\omega$ with the first-stage indicators shared across scenarios and the
bounds of \eqref{eq:bnd_pd} taken at their scenario values. Four of
them couple the two stages,
\begin{align}
&d_{jt}^{G,sc,\omega}=\tilde d_{jt}^{G,sc,\omega}+c_G^{sb}z_{jt}^{G,sb},
\label{eq:sup_decomp}\\
&\underline D_{jt}^{G}\le d_{jt}^{G,sc,\omega}\le\overline D_{jt}^{G},
\label{eq:sup_window}\\
&\underline d^{G}z_{jt}^{G,on}\le\tilde d_{jt}^{G,sc,\omega}-r_{jt}^{u,\mathrm{els},\omega},
\nonumber\\
&\tilde d_{jt}^{G,sc,\omega}+r_{jt}^{d,\mathrm{els},\omega}\le\overline d^{G}z_{jt}^{G,on},
\label{eq:sup_elsres}\\
&z_{jt}^{G,on}=\ssum_{l\in L}\hat z_{jlt}^{\omega},\qquad
 \tilde d_{jt}^{G,sc,\omega}=\ssum_{l\in L}\hat d_{jlt}^{\omega},
\label{eq:sup_pwl}
\end{align}
\end{subequations}
where $\underline D_{jt}^{G},\overline D_{jt}^{G}$ are the window
\eqref{eq:window}, which depends on the first-stage indicators alone. The
last of these is where non-anticipativity is visible: the unit is on or
off in every scenario alike, while the operating segment is chosen after
the realization.
\subsection{Compact Form}
Stack the second-stage variables of prosumer $j$ as
$x_j=(x_j^{\omega})_{\omega\in\Omega}$ and its binaries as
$y_j=\big(z_j,(\hat z_j^{\omega})_{\omega\in\Omega}\big)$. The
prosumer-level constraints are then
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}}=\big\{(x_j,y_j):\ T_jx_j+W_jy_j\le h_j\big\},
\label{eq:sup_Xmip}
\end{equation}
which is \eqref{eq:Xmip} of the main paper with $T_j$ and $W_j$
block-diagonal over $\Omega$ and with the rows
\eqref{eq:sup_decomp}--\eqref{eq:sup_pwl} tying $z_j$ to every block. It
is bounded, since \eqref{eq:bnd_trade} bounds each scenario block, and
mixed-integer linear representable. The objective terms of prosumer $j$,
\begin{equation}
f_j(x_j,y_j)=\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}f_j^{\omega}
\big(x_j^{\omega},\hat z_j^{\omega}\big)
-\ssum_{t\in T}c_j^{G,su}z_{jt}^{G,su},
\label{eq:sup_fj}
\end{equation}
are linear. Within a scenario each price multiplies a variable carrying
the same scenario index, so no product of two variables appears; the
objective would become bilinear only if the community set the prices,
which Assumption~\ref{as:env}(ii) excludes. The community-level variables
and costs are
\begin{align}
&x_0=\big((r_i^{sym})_{i\in I},(p^{\omega})_{\omega\in\Omega}\big)\ge0 \nonumber,\\
&c_0=\big((\bar\pi_i^{res})_{i},(-\rho_{\omega}\delta^{peak})_{\omega}\big),
\label{eq:sup_x0}
\end{align}
and $x_0$ appears on the left-hand side of
\eqref{eq:sup_bal}--\eqref{eq:sup_peak} only. Stacking those rows, each
equality as a pair of inequalities, gives
$\ssum_{j\in S}A_jx_j+A_0x_0\le\ssum_{j\in S}b_j$ with $b_j=0$ and
\begin{equation}
m=\underbrace{2|K||T||\Omega|}_{\eqref{eq:sup_bal}}
+\underbrace{2|T||\Omega|}_{\eqref{eq:sup_res}}
+\underbrace{|T||\Omega|}_{\eqref{eq:sup_peak}}
=(2|K|+3)|T||\Omega| .
\label{eq:sup_m}
\end{equation}
Both sides are additive over the members, so Assumption~\ref{as:pool}
holds. No price appears in \eqref{eq:sup_bal}--\eqref{eq:sup_peak}. The
linking rows, and with them $A_j$, $A_0$ and the count $m$, are the same
whether prices are known or not.
\subsection{Relaxation and Reformulation}
Dualizing \eqref{eq:sup_bal}--\eqref{eq:sup_peak} with $\theta\ge0$, the
contribution of $x_0$ is finite only on
$\Theta=\{\theta\ge0:A_0^{\top}\theta\ge c_0\}$, which reads
\begin{align}
&\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\ssum_{t\in T_i}
\big(\mu_t^{u,\omega}+\mu_t^{d,\omega}\big)\ge\bar\pi_i^{res}\ \ \forall i,
\nonumber \\
&\ssum_{t\in T}\xi_t^{\omega}\le\rho_{\omega}\delta^{peak}\ \ \forall\omega .
\label{eq:sup_Theta}
\end{align}
The relaxation then separates as in \eqref{eq:vlr_sep}, with
\begin{equation}
\vlr_j(\theta)=\max_{(x_j,y_j)\in\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}}}
\big\{f_j(x_j,y_j)-\theta^{\top}A_jx_j\big\},
\label{eq:sup_vlrj}
\end{equation}
a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program of a single prosumer.
Let $Q_j$ index the extreme points of
$\conv(\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}})$. A column $q\in Q_j$ is a complete
contingent plan $\big(z_j^{q},(x_j^{\omega,q},\hat z_j^{\omega,q})_{\omega}\big)$,
with expected profit $w_j^{q}=f_j(\cdot^{q})$ and linking contribution
$a_j^{q}=A_jx_j^{q}\in\R^{m}$. The relaxed master is
\begin{subequations}\label{eq:sup_dwr}
\begin{align}
&(\mathrm{DWR}_S^{\Omega}):\ \max\
\ssum_{j\in S}\ssum_{q\in Q_j}w_j^{q}\lambda_j^{q}
+\ssum_{i\in I}\bar\pi_i^{res}r_i^{sym} \nonumber\\
&\hspace{10.5em}-\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}\delta^{peak}p^{\omega}
\label{eq:sup_dwr_obj}\\
&\mathrm{s.t.}\ \ssum_{j\in S}\ssum_{q\in Q_j}
\big(i_{jt}^{k,com,\omega,q}-e_{jt}^{k,com,\omega,q}\big)\lambda_j^{q}=0,
\ \ \forall t,k,\omega
\label{eq:sup_dwr_bal}\\
&\hspace{1.7em} r_i^{sym}\le\ssum_{j\in S}\ssum_{q\in Q_j}
 r_{jt}^{u/d,\omega,q}\lambda_j^{q},
\ \ \forall i,\,t\in T_i,\,\omega
\label{eq:sup_dwr_res}\\
&\hspace{1.7em} \ssum_{j\in S}\ssum_{q\in Q_j}
 \big(i_{jt}^{E,mkt,\omega,q}-e_{jt}^{E,mkt,\omega,q}\big)\lambda_j^{q}\le p^{\omega},
\nonumber\\
&\hspace{12em}\forall t,\omega
\label{eq:sup_dwr_peak}\\
&\hspace{1.7em} \ssum_{q\in Q_j}\lambda_j^{q}=1,\quad \forall j\in S
\dual{\sigma_j} \label{eq:sup_dwr_conv}\\
&\hspace{1.7em} \lambda_j^{q}\ge0,\quad x_0\ge0, \label{eq:sup_dwr_nn}
\end{align}
\end{subequations}
the first three rows holding for every index of
\eqref{eq:sup_bal}--\eqref{eq:sup_peak}. A column is a contingent plan,
so no non-anticipativity row is needed and the plan priced out at the
optimal duals can serve as a settlement basis, which the next subsection
uses.

\subsection{Allocations under Uncertainty}
\label{sec:sup_alloc}
An allocation of expected surplus leaves open what each member is paid
once a scenario is realized, and need not balance the community's books
in any single scenario. The stochastic cooperative game of Suijs
\emph{et al.}~\cite{suijs1999cooperative}, in the form of
Uhan~\cite{uhan2015stochastic}, separates the two questions.

\begin{definition}[\cite{uhan2015stochastic}]
\label{def:sup_uhan}
An \emph{allocation} for $S\subseteq N$ is a pair
$(x,a)\in\R^{S\times\Omega}\times A_S$, with $A_S$ the first-stage
actions of $S$ and $v(S,a,\omega)$ its worth in scenario $\omega$, such
that
\begin{equation}
\ssum_{j\in S}x_j(\omega)\le v(S,a,\omega),\qquad\forall\omega\in\Omega ;
\label{eq:sup_uhan_feas}
\end{equation}
$Z_S$ denotes the set of such pairs. With member $j$ ranking random
payoffs by a certainty equivalent $\phi_j$, the \emph{certainty
equivalent game} is
$v^{\phi}(S)=\max_{(x,a)\in Z_S}\ssum_{j\in S}\phi_j\big((x,a)_j\big)$,
and the \emph{weak $\varepsilon$-core} of the stochastic game is the set
of $(x,a)\in Z_N$ with
\begin{equation}
\ssum_{j\in S}\phi_j\big((x,a)_j\big)\ \ge\ v^{\phi}(S)-|S|\varepsilon
\quad\forall S\subseteq N,
\label{eq:sup_stochcore}
\end{equation}
with equality at $S=N$; at $\varepsilon=0$ this is the core
of~\cite{uhan2015stochastic}.
\end{definition}

The payment may depend on the scenario arbitrarily and the budget must
balance in each scenario, but the deviation test is taken once, before
the realization. Imposing it at every stage instead gives the strong
sequential core of~\cite{toriello2017dynamic}, which we do not address.

Write $SU_j(z_j)=\ssum_{t\in T}c_j^{G,su}z_{jt}^{G,su}$ and
$a=\big((z_j)_{j\in S},(r_i^{sym})_{i\in I}\big)$. Under
\eqref{eq:sup_uhan_feas} the first-stage terms enter the worth of every
scenario in full, so
\begin{align}
&v^{\Omega}(S,a,\omega):=\ssum_{i\in I}\bar\pi_i^{res}r_i^{sym}
-\ssum_{j\in S}SU_j(z_j) \nonumber\\
&+\max\Big\{\ssum_{j\in S}f_j^{\omega}\big(x_j^{\omega},\hat z_j^{\omega}\big)
-\delta^{peak}p^{\omega}:\eqref{eq:sup_bal}\text{--}\eqref{eq:sup_peak}
\nonumber\\
&\hspace{5.4em}\text{at }\omega,\ \text{recourse feasible given }a\Big\},
\label{eq:sup_worth}
\end{align}
and, the recourse decoupling across scenarios once $a$ is fixed,
$\max_{a\in A_S}\ssum_{\omega}\rho_{\omega}v^{\Omega}(S,a,\omega)
=\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_S^{\Omega})$. The first-stage terms are thus
carried in full by each scenario rather than apportioned over them. Note
that $v^{\Omega}$ is a gross worth while $\Gamma^{\mathrm{MIP}}$ is
normalized by \eqref{eq:v0}, a constant per member.

Since \eqref{eq:sup_vlrj} is a mixed-integer program it returns no
multipliers of its own, only an integer contingent plan; the prices are
the master's. The two together determine a scenario-dependent
allocation.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sup_scen}
Let $\theta^{*},\{\sigma_j^{*}\}$ be optimal duals of \eqref{eq:sup_dwr}
with $S=N$, let $q_j^{*}$ attain \eqref{eq:sup_vlrj} at $\theta^{*}$, and
let $\hat a$ be the first-stage part of an optimal solution of
$(\mathrm{DP}_N^{\Omega})$. With
$\bar\theta^{\omega}=\theta^{*\omega}/\rho_{\omega}$, put
\begin{align}
\chi_j^{\Omega}(\omega)&=f_j^{\omega}\big(x_j^{\omega,q^{*}},\hat z_j^{\omega,q^{*}}\big)
-\bar\theta^{\omega\top}A_j^{\omega}x_j^{\omega,q^{*}}-SU_j\big(z_j^{q^{*}}\big),
\label{eq:sup_chiscen}\\
g^{\omega}&=\ssum_{j\in N}\chi_j^{\Omega}(\omega)-v^{\Omega}(N,\hat a,\omega),
\qquad
x_j^{*}=\chi_j^{\Omega}-g^{\omega}/n .
\label{eq:sup_resid}
\end{align}
If the members are risk neutral, $\phi_j=\mathbb{E}$, then
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $v^{\phi}(S)=\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_S^{\Omega})$, so the
certainty equivalent game is $\Gamma^{\mathrm{MIP}}$ up to the
normalization \eqref{eq:v0};
\item[(b)] $(x^{*},\hat a)\in Z_N$ with equality in
\eqref{eq:sup_uhan_feas} in every scenario, and
$\mathbb{E}[x_j^{*}]=\sigma_j^{*}-\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}/n$;
\item[(c)] if
$\chi_j:=\mathbb{E}[x_j^{*}]-\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_{\{j\}}^{\Omega})$
lies in the weak $\varepsilon$-core of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{MIP}}$, then
$(x^{*},\hat a)$ lies in the weak $\varepsilon$-core of the stochastic
game.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{IEEEproof}
(a) With $\phi_j=\mathbb{E}$ the objective of the certainty equivalent
game is $\ssum_{\omega}\rho_{\omega}\ssum_{j\in S}x_j(\omega)$, which
\eqref{eq:sup_uhan_feas} bounds by
$\ssum_{\omega}\rho_{\omega}v^{\Omega}(S,a,\omega)$ and which saturating
it attains; maximizing over $a$ gives the claim.

(b) $T_j,W_j,A_j$ are block diagonal over $\Omega$ and $SU_j$ carries no
scenario index, so $\ssum_{\omega}\rho_{\omega}\chi_j^{\Omega}(\omega)
=f_j(\cdot^{q^{*}})-\theta^{*\top}A_jx_j^{q^{*}}=\vlr_j(\theta^{*})
=\sigma_j^{*}$. Hence
$\ssum_{\omega}\rho_{\omega}g^{\omega}
=\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DWR}_N^{\Omega})-\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_N^{\Omega})
=\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}$, which gives the expectation, and summing
\eqref{eq:sup_resid} over $j$ gives the scenario-wise equality.

(c) Adding $\ssum_{j\in S}\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_{\{j\}}^{\Omega})$ to
both sides of the weak $\varepsilon$-core inequality for $\chi$ turns it,
by (a), into \eqref{eq:sup_stochcore}; equality at $S=N$ is (b) in
expectation. The passage from the certainty equivalent game to the
stochastic game is \cite[Prop.~2.2(b)]{uhan2015stochastic}, which uses
nothing beyond translation invariance of $\phi_j$ and so tolerates the
relaxation by $|S|\varepsilon$.
\end{IEEEproof}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sup_scen} collects the construction. Lines~1--3 are
the procedure of Section~\ref{sec:complexity} unchanged, the plans
$q_j^{*}$ being the columns priced out in its terminal iteration; the
rest is $O(n|\Omega|)$ arithmetic on quantities already returned.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Scenario-dependent allocation}
\label{alg:sup_scen}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE $\Omega$, $\{\rho_{\omega}\}$,
 $\{\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}},f_j\}_{j\in N}$, linking rows
 \eqref{eq:sup_bal}--\eqref{eq:sup_peak}
\ENSURE $\{x_j^{*}(\omega)\}$, $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LR}}$
\STATE Solve $(\mathrm{DWR}_N^{\Omega})$ by column generation; retain
 $\theta^{*}$ and $\{\sigma_j^{*}\}$
\STATE Retain, for each $j$, the terminal priced column $q_j^{*}$
 attaining \eqref{eq:sup_vlrj} at $\theta^{*}$
\STATE Solve $(\mathrm{DP}_N^{\Omega})$; retain its first-stage part
 $\hat a$
\STATE $\bar\theta^{\omega}\leftarrow\theta^{*\omega}/\rho_{\omega}$
\FOR{$\omega\in\Omega$}
  \STATE $\chi_j^{\Omega}(\omega)\leftarrow$ \eqref{eq:sup_chiscen},
   $j\in N$
  \STATE $g^{\omega}\leftarrow\ssum_{j\in N}\chi_j^{\Omega}(\omega)
   -v^{\Omega}(N,\hat a,\omega)$
  \STATE $x_j^{*}(\omega)\leftarrow\chi_j^{\Omega}(\omega)-g^{\omega}/n$,
   $j\in N$
\ENDFOR
\STATE $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LR}}\leftarrow
 \ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}g^{\omega}/n$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

One hypothesis is left open, that $\chi$ lies in the weak
$\varepsilon$-core of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{MIP}}$ for an $\varepsilon$ worth
reporting. By part~(b),
$\chi_j=\sigma_j^{*}-\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_{\{j\}}^{\Omega})
-\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}/n$, which is the allocation $\chi^{\mathrm{LR}}$ of
the main paper; the rest of this section discharges the hypothesis.

\subsection{Stability of the Allocation}
\label{sec:sup_stab}
The constant $\bar\gamma$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:eps} is measured on
the scenario-expanded loss. For $j\in N$ and
$\bar x_j\in\conv(\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}})$, let
$\bar a_j^{\mathrm{bal}}=(\bar a_{jt}^{k,bal,\omega})_{k,t,\omega}$ be
its net community position in every carrier, period and scenario, let
$\mathcal{X}_j(\bar a_j^{\mathrm{bal}})$ be the schedules of $j$
attaining that position in every $(k,t,\omega)$, and write
$\bar w_j$, $\bar r_{jt}^{u,\omega},\bar r_{jt}^{d,\omega}$ and
$\bar n_{jt}^{E,\omega}$ for the expected objective value, the reserve
contributions and the net market imports of $\bar x_j$, and
$w_j(x)$, $r_{jt}^{u,\omega}(x),r_{jt}^{d,\omega}(x)$,
$n_{jt}^{E,\omega}(x)$ for the same quantities at $x$. With
$\bar\Pi^{res}:=\ssum_{i\in I}\bar\pi_i^{res}$, put
\begin{align}
&L_j^{\Omega}(x):=\big(\bar w_j-w_j(x)\big)^{+} \nonumber\\
&+\bar\Pi^{res}\max_{t\in T,\,\omega\in\Omega}\max\big\{
 \big(\bar r_{jt}^{u,\omega}-r_{jt}^{u,\omega}(x)\big)^{+},\,
 \big(\bar r_{jt}^{d,\omega}-r_{jt}^{d,\omega}(x)\big)^{+}\big\} \nonumber\\
&+\delta^{peak}\ssum_{\omega\in\Omega}\rho_{\omega}\max_{t\in T}
 \big(n_{jt}^{E,\omega}(x)-\bar n_{jt}^{E,\omega}\big)^{+},
\label{eq:sup_Lj}
\end{align}
and define $\tilde\gamma_j$ and $\bar\gamma$ by \eqref{eq:gammatilde}
with $L_j^{\Omega}$ in place of $L_j$ and
$\mathcal{X}_j(\bar a_j^{\mathrm{bal}})$ as above. The reserve rows
\eqref{eq:sup_res} are imposed in every scenario, so a shortfall
anywhere in $T_i\times\Omega$ caps $r_i^{sym}$ for the whole block,
which is why that term is a maximum over $t$ and $\omega$ and not a sum;
the peak enters once per scenario and is charged in expectation, which
is why the last term is.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:sup_stoch}
For the model \eqref{eq:sup_dp}, Assumption~\ref{as:pool} holds, and
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Lemma~\ref{lem:lpg} applies to \eqref{eq:sup_dwr}, so the
Lagrangian sub-game is a linear production game, and since $b_j=0$ its
Owen solution is $\sigma_j^{*}$. The allocation \eqref{eq:chi_ow} of
$\Gamma^{\mathrm{MIP}}$ is then
$\chi_j^{\mathrm{OW}}=\sigma_j^{*}-\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{DP}_{\{j\}}^{\Omega})$,
the stand-alone term being the scenario-expanded single-member problem;
\item[(b)] Proposition~\ref{prop:opap} and Corollary~\ref{cor:eps} hold.
\item[(c)] Proposition~\ref{prop:eps} holds with $m$ given by
\eqref{eq:sup_m} and with $\bar\gamma$ measured on \eqref{eq:sup_Lj},
which is independent of $|\Omega|$ under the price support fixed in
Section~\ref{sec:sup_stages}, so
\begin{equation}
\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LR}}\le\frac{(m+1)\bar\gamma}{n}
=O\!\left(\frac{|T||\Omega|}{n}\right).
\label{eq:sup_bound}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{IEEEproof}
Assumption~\ref{as:pool} was verified after \eqref{eq:sup_m}, and
\eqref{eq:sup_Xmip}--\eqref{eq:sup_x0} place the model in the form the
proofs of the main paper use, so (a) and (b) follow with no change of
argument. For (c), the construction of Proposition~\ref{prop:eps} is
repeated with $L_j^{\Omega}$, and only two points require comment.

First, $\mathcal{X}_j(\bar a_j^{\mathrm{bal}})$ is nonempty. Take any
$(x_j,y_j)\in\mathcal{X}_j^{\mathrm{MIP}}$, keep its first-stage
indicators and its physical variables, and in each scenario set the
community trades to $\bar a_j^{\mathrm{bal}}$ and close
\eqref{eq:pb_E}--\eqref{eq:pb_GH} with the market trades, which
\eqref{eq:bnd_size} admits scenario by scenario. Neither the community
nor the market trades enter the commitment rows
\eqref{eq:sup_decomp}--\eqref{eq:sup_pwl}, so feasibility is preserved.

Second, each term of \eqref{eq:sup_Lj} is bounded independently of
$|\Omega|$. The objective enters as the expectation \eqref{eq:sup_fj},
whose value is bounded by the capacities of $j$ and by
$\max_{t,k,\omega}\pi_t^{k,imkt,\omega}$ because
$\ssum_{\omega}\rho_{\omega}=1$ and the prices lie in a fixed compact
set, so refining the scenario set enlarges neither. The reserve term is
a maximum over $t$, over the two directions and over $\omega$, and not a
sum, hence bounded by the reserve capacity of $j$. The peak term is an
expectation over $\omega$ of a maximum over $t$, bounded by the trade
bounds \eqref{eq:bnd_trade} for the same reason. Hence $\bar\gamma$ is
finite and depends on the assets of $j$ alone. The Shapley--Folkman
argument is then applied in $\R^{m+1}$ with $m$ as in \eqref{eq:sup_m}.
\end{IEEEproof}

Part~(b) is the hypothesis of Lemma~\ref{lem:sup_scen}(c) at
$\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LR}}$. The pair $(x^{*},\hat a)$ of
\eqref{eq:sup_resid} therefore settles in every scenario and lies in the
weak $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LR}}$-core of the stochastic game, with
$\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LR}}$ bounded by \eqref{eq:sup_bound}.

\begin{remark}[The bound is one-sided in $|\Omega|$]
The factor $|\Omega|$ in \eqref{eq:sup_bound} enters through $m$, the
number of linking rows, and bounds the number of members that
Shapley--Folkman leaves at a fractional schedule. It should not be read
as a statement about $\omega^{\mathrm{LR}}$ itself. A finite $\Omega$ is
a discretization of an underlying distribution, and refining it makes
$(\mathrm{DP}_S^{\Omega})$ and $(\mathrm{DWR}_S^{\Omega})$ approach the
problems it approximates, so the gap between them has no reason to grow
with the number of scenarios while the bound does. What
\eqref{eq:sup_bound} supports is the same structural statement as in the
deterministic case, that the count of fractional members is set by the
linking rows and not by $n$, and the decay in $n$ that follows from it.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the allocation]
\label{rem:sup_scen}
Settling scenario by scenario strengthens no stability statement.
Definition~\ref{def:sup_uhan} tests deviation before the realization, so
a coalition preferring to leave after observing $\omega$ is not ruled
out, and \eqref{eq:sup_bound} bounds a tolerance in expectation: the
residuals $g^{\omega}$ are individually unsigned and admit no
per-scenario counterpart. Nor is the construction unique, as
\eqref{eq:sup_vlrj} may have several maximizers at $\theta^{*}$, each
giving a different $\chi_j^{\Omega}$ of the same expectation. Under risk
neutrality the choice is immaterial, only the expectation entering
$v^{\phi}$; for risk-averse members it would have to be made, $v^{\phi}$
then departing from $\Gamma^{\mathrm{MIP}}$.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Cost of the extension]
The pricing problem \eqref{eq:sup_vlrj} remains one mixed-integer program
per prosumer, of $|\Omega|$ times the size of its deterministic
counterpart, and the $n$ of them stay independent. The separation
\eqref{eq:rg_sep} of the row generation grows by the same factor while
remaining a single monolithic program, so the comparison of
Table~\ref{tab:complexity} is unaffected. Algorithm~\ref{alg:sup_scen}
adds nothing to either column of that table, reusing the duals and
columns the reformulation has already produced.
\end{remark}

% \label{sec:sup_eps}
% Fix an allocation $\chi\in\R^{n}$ of the value of the grand coalition
% among the members $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$. Its worst per-capita excess is
% \begin{equation}
% \varepsilon(\chi)\;=\;\max_{\emptyset\neq S\subsetneq N}\
% \frac{v(S)-\ssum_{j\in S}\chi_j}{|S|},
% \label{eq:sup_pcexcess}
% \end{equation}
% so that $\varepsilon(\chi)\le 0$ certifies $\chi\in\mathcal{C}(v)$ and,
% more generally, $\varepsilon(\chi)\le\bar\varepsilon$ certifies
% $\chi\in\mathcal{C}_{\bar\varepsilon}(v)$. This is the quantity reported
% for $\chi^{\mathrm{LR}}$ in the main paper.
% Two things make \eqref{eq:sup_pcexcess} hard. The feasible set has
% $2^{n}-2$ elements, and each evaluation of the numerator requires
% $v(S)$, hence a unit-commitment dispatch of the coalition. Enumeration is out of reach, so the maximization has to be
% carried out implicitly.
% \subsection{A Single Mixed-Integer Fractional Program}
% Introduce $z\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ with $S(z)=\{j\in N:z_j=1\}$, and let $x$
% collect the dispatch variables of the community model, continuous and
% binary. Write $X(z)$ for the dispatch feasible set in which every
% variable belonging to a member $j$ with $z_j=0$ is forced to zero, and
% $\pi^{\top}x$ for the dispatch objective, so that
% \begin{equation}
% \vdp{S(z)}\;=\;\max_{x\in X(z)}\ \pi^{\top}x ,
% \label{eq:sup_inner}
% \end{equation}
% and, by Definition~\ref{def:game},
% $v(S(z))=\vdp{S(z)}-\ssum_{j\in N}\vdp{\{j\}}z_j$.
% The nesting in \eqref{eq:sup_pcexcess} collapses. The numerator contains
% $\vdp{S}$ with a positive sign, and $\vdp{S}$ is itself a maximum, so
% the outer maximization over $S$ and the inner maximization over $x$ are
% maxima of the same expression and can be merged into one. Writing
% $\hchi_j:=\chi_j+\vdp{\{j\}}$ for the payoff of $j$ gross of its
% stand-alone value and putting
% \begin{equation}
% \mathcal{N}(z,x)=\pi^{\top}x-\ssum_{j\in N}\hchi_j z_j,
% \quad
% \mathcal{D}(z)=\ssum_{j\in N} z_j,
% \label{eq:sup_numden}
% \end{equation}
% and
% \begin{equation}
% \begin{split}
% \Omega=\Big\{(z,x)\ :\ &z\in\{0,1\}^{n},\ x\in X(z),\\
% &1\le\ssum_{j\in N}z_j\le n-1\Big\},
% \end{split}
% \label{eq:sup_omega}
% \end{equation}
% we obtain
% \begin{equation}
% \varepsilon(\chi)\;=\;\max_{(z,x)\in\Omega}\
% \frac{\mathcal{N}(z,x)}{\mathcal{D}(z)} .
% \label{eq:sup_mifp}
% \end{equation}
% The bounds in \eqref{eq:sup_omega} exclude $S=\emptyset$ and $S=N$ and
% also guarantee $\mathcal{D}(z)\ge 1>0$ throughout, which is what the
% fractional program requires.
% Problem \eqref{eq:sup_mifp} is a mixed-integer linear fractional
% program. Both $\mathcal{N}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are affine, the
% deactivation of a non-member is expressed by big-$M$ inequalities rather
% than by products $z_j x_j$, and the nonlinear conversion efficiencies
% are represented by a disaggregated piecewise-linear formulation with
% segment binaries. No product of two variables appears anywhere, so
% $\Omega$ is a mixed-integer linear set. This is not a matter of
% convenience. It is what makes the certificate of
% Section~\ref{sec:sup_conv} available, since a global maximum over
% $\Omega$ is what branch and bound delivers and what a nonconvex
% mixed-integer nonlinear formulation would not.
% \subsection{The Dinkelbach Transform}
% Following Dinkelbach \cite{dinkelbach1967}, associate with
% \eqref{eq:sup_mifp} the parametric problem
% \begin{equation}
% F(\lambda)\;=\;\max_{(z,x)\in\Omega}\
% \big\{\mathcal{N}(z,x)-\lambda\,\mathcal{D}(z)\big\},
% \label{eq:sup_Flambda}
% \end{equation}
% defined for every $\lambda\in\R$.
% \begin{proposition}\label{prop:sup_F}
% $F$ is convex and strictly decreasing, and its unique root is
% $\varepsilon(\chi)$. That is, $F(\lambda)>0$ if and only if
% $\lambda<\varepsilon(\chi)$, $F(\lambda)=0$ if and only if
% $\lambda=\varepsilon(\chi)$, and $F(\lambda)<0$ if and only if
% $\lambda>\varepsilon(\chi)$.
% \end{proposition}
% \begin{IEEEproof}
% For fixed $(z,x)$ the map
% $\lambda\mapsto\mathcal{N}(z,x)-\lambda\mathcal{D}(z)$ is affine with
% slope $-\mathcal{D}(z)\le-1$. $F$ is the pointwise maximum of these
% affine functions over the finite set $\Omega$, hence convex and strictly
% decreasing. For the root, $F(\lambda)\ge 0$ holds if and only if some
% $(z,x)\in\Omega$ has $\mathcal{N}(z,x)/\mathcal{D}(z)\ge\lambda$, that
% is, if and only if $\varepsilon(\chi)\ge\lambda$, and $F(\lambda)\le 0$
% holds if and only if every $(z,x)$ has
% $\mathcal{N}(z,x)/\mathcal{D}(z)\le\lambda$, that is, if and only if
% $\varepsilon(\chi)\le\lambda$.
% \end{IEEEproof}
% Computing $\varepsilon(\chi)$ is therefore root finding on $F$, and
% Newton's method on a convex decreasing function is exactly Dinkelbach's
% iteration. Choose any $(z_0,x_0)\in\Omega$ and set
% $\lambda_1=\mathcal{N}(z_0,x_0)/\mathcal{D}(z_0)$. At iteration
% $k=1,2,\dots$, solve \eqref{eq:sup_Flambda} at $\lambda_k$ to global
% optimality and obtain a maximizer $(z_k,x_k)$ together with the value
% $F(\lambda_k)$. If $F(\lambda_k)\le 0$ the method stops and
% $\lambda_k=\varepsilon(\chi)$. Otherwise set
% $\lambda_{k+1}=\mathcal{N}(z_k,x_k)/\mathcal{D}(z_k)$ and repeat.
% \subsection{The Parametric Subproblem Is the Original Separation}
% The step that makes the scheme practical is that
% \eqref{eq:sup_Flambda} is not a new model. Substituting
% \eqref{eq:sup_numden},
% \begin{equation}
% \begin{split}
% \mathcal{N}(z,x)-\lambda\,\mathcal{D}(z)
% &=\pi^{\top}x-\ssum_{j\in N}\hchi_j z_j-\lambda\ssum_{j\in N}z_j\\
% &=\pi^{\top}x-\ssum_{j\in N}\big(\hchi_j+\lambda\big)z_j .
% \end{split}
% \label{eq:sup_shift}
% \end{equation}
% Because $|S|$ is linear in $z$, the term $\lambda\mathcal{D}(z)$ is
% absorbed into the objective coefficients of the very binaries that
% define $S$. The parametric problem at $\lambda$ is thus the raw-excess
% separation
% \begin{equation}
% \max_{S\subseteq N}\ \Big\{v(S)-\ssum_{j\in S}\chi'_j\Big\},
% \quad \chi'_j=\chi_j+\lambda ,
% \label{eq:sup_sep}
% \end{equation}
% which is the separation problem of the row-generation scheme of the main
% paper. It is the same mixed-integer program with the same variables,
% constraints and big-$M$ structure, and differs only in $n$ objective
% coefficients, each shifted by a common $\lambda$. Every Dinkelbach
% iteration therefore costs one separation solve and no more.
% \begin{remark}
% A denominator nonlinear in $z$ would break this. The reduction in
% \eqref{eq:sup_shift} is available precisely because the cardinality
% $|S|=\ssum_{j\in N}z_j$ is affine in the incidence vector.
% \end{remark}
% \subsection{Convergence and Early Termination}
% \label{sec:sup_conv}
% \begin{proposition}\label{prop:sup_conv}
% If every parametric problem \eqref{eq:sup_Flambda} is solved to global
% optimality, the sequence $(\lambda_k)$ is strictly increasing until it
% stops, satisfies $\lambda_k\le\varepsilon(\chi)$ for all $k$, and
% reaches $\varepsilon(\chi)$ after finitely many iterations.
% \end{proposition}
% \begin{IEEEproof}
% Each $\lambda_{k+1}$ is the ratio attained by the feasible point
% $(z_k,x_k)$, so $\lambda_{k+1}\le\varepsilon(\chi)$ by
% \eqref{eq:sup_mifp}. If the method does not stop at iteration $k$ then
% $F(\lambda_k)>0$, that is,
% $\mathcal{N}(z_k,x_k)-\lambda_k\mathcal{D}(z_k)>0$, and dividing by
% $\mathcal{D}(z_k)\ge 1$ gives $\lambda_{k+1}>\lambda_k$. The set
% $\Omega$ contains finitely many distinct values of $z$, so the ratios in
% \eqref{eq:sup_mifp} take finitely many values and a strictly increasing
% sequence drawn from them terminates. At termination $F(\lambda_k)\le 0$,
% which together with $\lambda_k\le\varepsilon(\chi)$ and
% Proposition~\ref{prop:sup_F} forces $\lambda_k=\varepsilon(\chi)$.
% \end{IEEEproof}
% Two consequences govern how a computed number may be read.
% \begin{remark}[One-sidedness]
% Every iterate is the ratio of an explicitly exhibited coalition, so
% $\lambda_k\le\varepsilon(\chi)$ holds whether or not the iteration ran
% to termination. A value returned by an interrupted run is therefore a
% valid lower bound on $\varepsilon(\chi)$ and nothing more. Consequently
% $\lambda_k>\bar\varepsilon$ refutes
% $\chi\in\mathcal{C}_{\bar\varepsilon}(v)$ even from an interrupted run,
% whereas $\lambda_k\le\bar\varepsilon$ establishes membership only if the
% run terminated. A nonpositive value read off a truncated measurement
% proves nothing.
% \end{remark}
% \begin{remark}[Where global optimality is needed]
% The proof uses global optimality of \eqref{eq:sup_Flambda} only in the
% stopping test. The inference from $F(\lambda_k)\le 0$ to
% $\lambda_k=\varepsilon(\chi)$ fails if the reported $F(\lambda_k)$ is
% merely a local or truncated maximum, since some unexplored $(z,x)$ may
% still carry a larger ratio. Monotonicity and the lower-bound property
% survive regardless, because they rest only on feasibility of the
% iterates.
% \end{remark}
% \begin{remark}[Sign convention]
% The formulation above follows the main paper, in which $v$ is a
% value to be maximized and a coalition blocks when
% $v(S)>\ssum_{j\in S}\chi_j$. Under the cost convention, in which
% values are negative for profit and a coalition blocks when it is charged
% more than it would pay alone, the numerator reads
% $\ssum_{j\in S}\chi_j-c(S)$ and the shift in \eqref{eq:sup_shift}
% becomes $\chi'_j=\chi_j-\lambda$. The two statements are equivalent.
% \end{remark}
